expert_context.text: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Selective-laser-melted Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy made from prealloyed powder. The as-printed material was a >97%-dense, single-fcc cellular microstructure with dislocation-rich cell walls; a comparison state was produced by direct aging and contained dual nanoprecipitates.
hidden_target.intervention: The study compared the oxidation behavior of the as-printed alloy with material aged at 750°C for 50 h. Aging produced approximately 25–30 vol% homogeneously distributed Ni/Ti-enriched L12 nanoscale precipitates and larger Al/Ti-enriched, Cr/Fe-depleted L21 precipitates, mainly near cell walls. Both states were then subjected to isothermal oxidation.
hidden_target.conditions: Polished 7.5 × 7.5 × 3 mm samples were oxidized for up to 96 h at 600, 750, 900, 1050, and 1200°C. Mass gain was monitored intermittently at 600–900°C, while oxide thickness was measured after 24, 48, 72, and 96 h at 900, 1050, and 1200°C. The reported atmosphere for oxidation was not explicitly specified.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: A duplex-to-trilayer oxide scale developed: an outer layer containing elemental and mixed/spinel oxides, a continuous homogeneous Cr-rich oxide (primarily Cr2O3) layer, and an inner discontinuous Al/Ti-rich oxide region. In the aged alloy, Cr-depleted precipitates and additional matrix–precipitate interfaces delayed formation of an equally protective Cr-oxide scale and provided possible short-circuit oxygen-diffusion paths.
hidden_target.mechanism: All constituent elements initially oxidized through loose or discontinuous surface oxides. With time, preferential outward Cr diffusion formed a dense Cr2O3 barrier that restricted inward oxygen and outward metal-ion diffusion, suppressing oxidation. Cr formed the continuous outer protective oxide despite Al and Ti having greater oxidation propensity because Cr has a smaller atomic size and more favorable mobility; Al3+ and Ti4+ have higher activation barriers/lower diffusivities and their low alloy concentrations inhibit continuous Al/Ti oxide layers. At higher temperatures, oxygen penetrated the Cr-rich scale through defects, microcracks, or grain-boundary channels, forming and thickening the inner Al/Ti-rich oxide region.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-printed baseline, precipitation-aged material was expected to show higher oxidation mass gain, particularly as temperature increased, because Cr-depleted precipitates and precipitate–matrix boundaries impair or delay formation of the protective Cr-oxide layer. Nevertheless, both states were expected to retain broadly similar high-temperature oxide-growth activation energies and Cr2O3-mediated protection, so aging would provide strengthening without a large overall oxidation penalty.
hidden_target.baseline: The baseline was the SLM as-printed, single-fcc cellular alloy with comparatively uniform Cr distribution and no L12/L21 nanoprecipitates; this uniform Cr distribution enabled earlier and easier formation of a protective Cr-rich oxide layer.
hidden_target.boundary: The Cr-rich scale provided effective protection at lower temperatures, generally up to about 900°C. Mass-gain kinetics were mainly subparabolic at 750–900°C, although behavior at 600°C was near parabolic and the aged alloy returned to near-parabolic behavior at 900°C. Above 900°C, oxide-thickness growth was nearly parabolic, and increasingly rapid oxygen transport produced a substantial inner inhomogeneous oxide layer. Results cover isothermal exposures of no more than 96 h and 600–1200°C.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: Time-resolved oxidation mass gain and power-law exponent/rate-constant fitting distinguished the two alloy states; cross-sectional SEM measurements quantified oxide-thickness growth and Arrhenius activation energies. SEM-EDS mapping identified elemental redistribution across the scale, while XRD and Raman spectroscopy identified Cr, Ti, elemental, and mixed/spinel oxides. Neutron diffraction and SEM characterized the initial fcc matrix and aged L12/L21 precipitates.
hidden_target.actual_result: The aged alloy consistently gained more mass than the as-printed alloy, with the difference becoming more pronounced with temperature, although absolute mass gains were not reported in the supplied text. Mass-gain exponents for as-printed material were n = 0.59, 0.33, and 0.26 at 600, 750, and 900°C, respectively; aged material gave n = 0.64, 0.26, and 0.59. Thus, both showed protective subparabolic behavior at 750°C, the as-printed alloy remained subparabolic at 900°C, and the aged alloy was near parabolic at 900°C. Oxide-thickness growth at 900–1200°C was nearly parabolic. Oxidation activation energies were very similar: 154.07 kJ/mol for as-printed and 152.83 kJ/mol for aged material, with pre-exponential factors of 22.74 × 10^6 and 10.98 × 10^6 μm/h^0.5, respectively. A continuous Cr-rich oxide layer significantly suppressed oxidation in both states, while the aged alloy retained its stated mechanical advantage without a significant overall increase in high-temperature oxidation degradation.

v3_queries.expert_context: Earlier oxidation studies on high-entropy alloys examined variations in Al, Cr, and Si content. Work on refractory and transition-metal-based systems reported benefits in some cases, but performance depended on composition, phase readjustment, and processing; Si was beneficial only within a limited range, while Al could alter phase constitution. These findings do not provide a general solution, as interactions among the many constituents make oxidation behavior complex, and recent studies of 3D-printed high-entropy alloys likewise showed that the degradation process remains difficult to interpret. For selective-laser-melted Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, any solution must retain the alloy’s mechanical performance and integrity during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases. What single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could overcome this limitation, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the as-printed alloy, defines the relevant exposure and material-state boundary conditions, relates the hypothesis to prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose outcome could falsify it?
